office: Mayor of the District of Columbia
scope_plain: Every DC voter. Ranked-choice: three candidates plus a write-in line, so you can rank up to 4 choices.
office_explainer: Runs the District's government: police, schools, housing, agencies, a $22 billion budget. Signs or vetoes Council laws.
why_it_matters: Open seat. Muriel Bowser is retiring after three terms, so DC picks a new mayor for the first time since 2014. The winner manages the city's relationship with Congress and the White House at a time of heavy federal involvement in DC affairs.

candidates.name: Rhonda Hamilton
candidates.background: Longtime ANC 6D commissioner (Southwest), small-business owner and mental health advocate who founded M.I. Mother's Keeper in 2015. Third-generation Washingtonian; left the Democratic Party in 2012. Ran a write-in campaign for mayor in 2022.

own_words.text: Wants to audit city agencies, starting with housing after a reported $52 million DC Housing Authority budget error, then MPD.
Opposes youth curfews: "Curfew, to me, means red flag because our governing body doesn't have any solution."
Priorities include housing stability, health care access, repairing community-police relationships and budget transparency.

candidates.name: Janeese Lewis George
candidates.background: Ward 4 councilmember since 2021 and a former prosecutor in the DC Attorney General's office. Won the June 16, 2026 Democratic primary with 54% in the final ranked-choice round; Kenyan McDuffie conceded. A member of Metro DC DSA.

own_words.text: "We're going to implement universal child care."
Campaign centers on "addressing the real affordability crisis we have in the city," including housing costs.
Wants more 911 call-takers, police focused on crime rather than immigration enforcement, and to push back on federal overreach.

candidates.name: Robert L. Gross
candidates.background: IT professional and civic activist who describes himself as a DC native, an eco-socialist and the Gen Z candidate. Won the Statehood Green primary in June.

own_words.text: "A central point of my campaign is the modernization of Washington, D.C. city government," using technology for budgeting, permits and real-time dashboards.
"We deserve a city shaped by those who live in it, not merely profit from it."

office: Chairman of the Council of the District of Columbia
scope_plain: Every DC voter. Two candidates, so this is a regular pick-one vote, not ranked-choice.
office_explainer: Leads the 13-member Council, sets its agenda and committees, and is next in line if the mayor leaves.
why_it_matters: The chair decides which bills move and runs the Council's budget process. Phil Mendelson has held the job since 2012 and would work with a new mayor from the Council's progressive wing.

candidates.name: Phil Mendelson
candidates.background: Council chairman since 2012; at-large councilmember from 1999. Unopposed in the June Democratic primary.

own_words.text: Running on his record, legislative experience and fiscal prudence (Hill Rag characterization; no 2026 general-election quote located).
Warned in a July 9 memo that at-large voters "may not meaningfully participate in the selection of both At-Large members" under the RCV count, and proposed a fix the Council later withdrew.

candidates.name: Abi-Ananiah Prudent
candidates.background: Nonprofit leader and community organizer who directs Concerned Women for America's DC work. Unopposed in the June Republican primary.

own_words.text: On keeping the IMPACT teacher evaluation system: "It's hard for me to understand why we'd want to take away something that's benefitting kids."
Campaign describes "strengthening families, supporting safe neighborhoods, and improving how local government serves residents."

office: At-Large Member of the Council of the District of Columbia
scope_plain: Every DC voter. TWO seats are filled. Ranked-choice: rank up to 5. Big gotcha: your ballot can only help elect ONE of the two winners. DCBOE counts each ballot once for your highest-ranked candidate still in the race and eliminates last place until two remain; once your top pick is one of the final two, your lower rankings never transfer. By the DC charter, only one of the two winners can be a Democrat. If you care which non-Democrat wins the second seat, rank that person first.
office_explainer: One of four citywide Council members who write DC laws and pass the budget.
why_it_matters: Two of four at-large seats. Anita Bonds (D) is retiring after 14 years. Elissa Silverman (I) won the June special election to finish Kenyan McDuffie's term and now seeks a full term. This is the first DC Council election counted with ranked-choice voting.

candidates.name: Oye Owolewa
candidates.background: Pharmacist and DC's shadow U.S. representative since 2021 (elected 2020). Ward 8 resident, former ANC 8E commissioner. Won the nine-way June Democratic primary with 50.8% in the final RCV round.

own_words.text: "I've dedicated my life in public service to leveling the playing field."
"Our budget needs to reflect what the 99% needs, not just the 1%."
Priorities: housing, education, jobs and stronger Council oversight.

candidates.name: Darryl Moch
candidates.background: Chair of the DC Statehood Green Party and a longtime social-justice advocate.

own_words.text: Priorities: housing, homelessness and LGBTQ issues (Hill Rag characterization; no direct quote located).
Party platform rests on a 'Human Life Standard' measuring government by outcomes in housing, safety, education and transparency.

candidates.name: Darrell Green
candidates.background: Lifelong DC resident, retired Metropolitan Police officer and former co-owner of an Adams Morgan bar. Not the former Washington football player.

own_words.text: On his top issue, truancy and schools: "Education, education, education."
Campaign describes "advocacy for safer communities, stronger neighborhoods, and practical leadership focused on residents' everyday concerns."

candidates.name: Elissa Silverman
candidates.background: At-large councilmember 2015 to 2023, then again since winning the June 16, 2026 special election (56%) to finish McDuffie's term. Former Washington Post and City Paper reporter and DC Fiscal Policy Institute analyst. Co-authored DC's paid family leave law.

own_words.text: "Elissa co-authored the District's paid family and medical leave law."
"Elissa has a strong track record of ensuring the District's $22 billion budget delivers programs that work."
Calls herself an innovator in making homes affordable for people of all income levels.

office: Delegate to the House of Representatives from the District of Columbia
scope_plain: Every DC voter. Ranked-choice: three candidates plus write-in, rank up to 4.
office_explainer: DC's non-voting member of Congress. Can introduce bills and vote in committee, not on the House floor.
why_it_matters: Open seat for the first time since 1990. Eleanor Holmes Norton is not running. The delegate is DC's main voice on statehood, home rule and federal moves against local laws.

candidates.name: Denise Rosado
candidates.background: Attorney and former federal advisor; has served at the FCC, as an Arizona assistant attorney general and as an administrative law judge. Unopposed in the June Republican primary.

own_words.text: Would de-emphasize statehood and push to exempt DC residents from federal income tax.
Campaign aims to "restore accountability, fiscal responsibility, and results-driven leadership to Washington, D.C."

candidates.name: Robert White
candidates.background: At-large councilmember since 2016 and former legislative counsel to Rep. Norton. Won the June Democratic primary with 64%.

own_words.text: "In Congress, I will fight every day to protect D.C.'s right to govern ourselves and to secure statehood."
"I will build coalitions, block harmful federal interference, and deliver resources that move our city forward."

candidates.name: Kymone Freeman
candidates.background: Co-founder of We Act Radio in Anacostia and the party's 2024 nominee for this seat.

own_words.text: "D.C. should not be paying federal income taxes in the absence of statehood."
Wants rent capped at 30% of income and to address root causes of violence.

office: Attorney General for the District of Columbia
scope_plain: Every DC voter. Two candidates, so a regular pick-one vote, not ranked-choice.
office_explainer: DC's top lawyer. Sues on the District's behalf, prosecutes juvenile and some misdemeanor cases, enforces consumer and tenant law.
why_it_matters: The AG decides which lawsuits DC brings, including against the federal government, and handles juvenile prosecutions. Schwalb has led several challenges to federal actions in DC.

candidates.name: Manuel Rivera
candidates.background: Puerto Rico-born attorney with nearly 40 years of practice in immigration, workers' rights and family law; small-business owner. A former lifelong Democrat who became a Republican after the 2024 election.

own_words.text: "Public safety, government accountability, taxes, and protecting our citizens are not just Republican or Democrat issues."
Names "juvenile crime, homelessness, drug addiction, family domestic violence" as his focus and criticizes Schwalb's lawsuits against the federal government.

candidates.name: Brian L. Schwalb
candidates.background: Attorney General since 2023; former partner at Venable. Won the June Democratic primary with 91%.

own_words.text: "I am committed to using the law to make DC safer, stronger and more affordable."
Will "seek swift and certain consequences for youth who commit violent offenses."
Priorities: consumer protection, housing and wage enforcement, juvenile justice, defending DC autonomy against federal actions.

scope_plain: Every DC voter. Two candidates, so a regular pick-one vote. The ballot just says 'United States Senator'; DC's shadow senators are not seated in the Senate.
office_explainer: Unpaid lobbyist for DC statehood. Not seated in the Senate; no vote. One of two shadow senators.
why_it_matters: A symbolic office DC voters created in 1990 to push for statehood. Six-year term. Paul Strauss has held it since 1997.

candidates.name: Robert Simmons
candidates.background: DC resident for more than 20 years, local business owner and founder of the nonprofit Global Alliance, Inc.

own_words.text: Campaign lists advocating for DC statehood and strengthening national security.
Priorities: congressional representation, public safety, fiscal accountability and federal cooperation.

candidates.name: Paul Strauss
candidates.background: Shadow senator since 1997, attorney and former ANC commissioner. Unopposed in the June Democratic primary.

own_words.text: Priorities: statehood and building support outside DC for admission as the 51st state (Hill Rag characterization; no 2026 quote located).
Background and record on Ballotpedia.

scope_plain: Every DC voter. Two candidates, so a regular pick-one vote. The ballot says 'United States Representative'; this is the unpaid shadow seat, not the Delegate.
office_explainer: Unpaid statehood advocate. Not seated in the House; no vote. Two-year term.
why_it_matters: Open seat. Oye Owolewa left it to run for Council. Like the shadow senators, this office exists to lobby Congress for DC statehood.
incumbent: Oye Owolewa (not running; running for Council at-large)

candidates.name: Ciprian Ivanof
candidates.background: Attorney (American University law) and former Army National Guard member, born in Romania, in DC 14 years. Second run for this seat.

own_words.text: Wants "to break up the dysfunctional culture of D.C. politics" and calls himself "a staunch advocate for economic freedom and education."
Argues the shadow delegation should scrutinize District management: public safety, education, WMATA, city finances.

candidates.name: Franklin Garcia
candidates.background: Held this seat 2015 to 2021 and founded the DC Latino Caucus. Unopposed in the June Democratic primary.

own_words.text: Seeking a return to the seat he held for six years to push for statehood (Hill Rag; no 2026 direct quote located).
Campaign site.
